title: Pediatric Procedural Sedation

body.text: Why this differs from the adult workflow

The core structure (pre-sedation risk screen → sedation → monitoring → recovery/discharge criteria — see procedural-sedation-workflow for that sequence, not restated here) is the same at any age. What's different in children: the drug of choice (ketamine dominates pediatric ED procedural sedation in a way it doesn't for adults), the NPO-status risk calculus, the monitoring intensity and equipment sizing, and a very common, usually benign recovery phenomenon (emergence agitation) that alarms families more than it should.
Ketamine — the pediatric ED sedation workhorse

Dissociative sedation with ketamine is the dominant choice for painful pediatric ED procedures (fracture/dislocation reduction, laceration repair, incision and drainage, foreign body removal) — favorable safety profile, preserves airway reflexes and respiratory drive better than most alternatives, and doesn't require IV access if given IM. This is a DIFFERENT dose and monitoring context from RSI-dose ketamine (see peds-ketamine-rsi / peds-rsi-decision-card) — procedural sedation doses are lower and the goal is dissociation with preserved spontaneous ventilation, not induction for paralysis and intubation.

items: IV route: 1-1.5 mg/kg initial dose, titrated; IM route: 3-4 mg/kg (useful when IV access is difficult or not otherwise needed for the procedure).

Co-administration of an antisialagogue (glycopyrrolate/atropine) is NOT routinely required — this was older teaching; current practice reserves it for a patient with a specific concern (excessive baseline secretions), not as a universal pretreatment.

Laryngospasm is the feared but rare complication — risk factors include younger age (especially under 2 years, particularly under 3 months), active respiratory tract infection, and airway manipulation/stimulation during deep dissociation; have suction and airway equipment ready regardless of perceived risk.

body.text: NPO status — a risk-modifying factor, not an absolute gate

Unlike elective anesthesia, ED procedural sedation frequently can't wait for a full NPO interval — the injury/condition needing sedation didn't wait for a convenient fasting window either. Current practice treats recent oral intake as ONE factor in the overall risk-benefit discussion (weighed against procedure urgency, sedation depth needed, and airway-reflex-preserving drug choice like ketamine), not an automatic delay-the-procedure rule. Document the discussion and the reasoning, and favor an airway-reflex-sparing approach (ketamine) over deep sedation with an agent that blunts protective reflexes when NPO status is a genuine concern.

items: Continuous pulse oximetry AND continuous capnography (end-tidal CO2) — capnography detects hypoventilation minutes before a pulse-oximetry desaturation would show up, especially important in a spontaneously-breathing sedated child where apnea can otherwise go unnoticed until oxygen reserve runs out.
Continuous cardiorespiratory/ECG monitoring and frequent blood pressure checks through the sedation and into early recovery.
Age/weight-appropriate resuscitation equipment (correctly sized airway equipment, weight-based emergency drug doses) available and checked BEFORE starting, not searched for if something goes wrong.
A dedicated provider whose only job is monitoring the sedation (not also performing the procedure) — this is a staffing/workflow point as important as any drug choice.

body.text: Recovery — emergence phenomena are common and usually benign

Emergence/recovery agitation (crying, thrashing, disorientation as the child wakes) is common with ketamine, especially in younger children, and is USUALLY self-limited and benign — it frightens families more than it indicates a real problem. A calm, dim, quiet recovery environment with a parent present when possible reduces it. Reserve treatment (small-dose benzodiazepine) for agitation that's severe, prolonged, or genuinely distressing rather than treating routine emergence reactions reflexively. Counsel families about this possibility BEFORE the sedation, not just when it happens — an informed parent handles it far better than a surprised one.
